text:
From the grassy saddle bivy, cross class 4 ramps to a shallow dihedral with a small tree in it, then continue to a dirt ledge at the base of a short wall. That dirt ledge is the start.

The small tree in the shallow dihedral is the discriminator. Miracle Ramps uses the same class 4 ramps but leads to a dihedral and then a starting wall ledge that it shares with this route's upper start, and the two only diverge higher; Nature's Way goes the other way, crossing the apron past Concerto's start to two-bolt ring anchors on the opposite wall.

This is an old-school ridge ramble: lichened overlaps and dirt-filled cracks low down are correct here, not evidence of being off route. The crux does not arrive until pitch 9.
runs: to a shallow dihedral with a small tree

text: The longer, more gradual way in from Icicle Creek Road: the Snow Lakes trail climbs past Nada and Snow lakes to Lake Vivianne, about ten miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain, looking straight at Prusik's south face. From Vivianne continue past the upper lakes to the base of the south face. It avoids the loose grind of Aasgard Pass at the cost of roughly two more miles and a thousand more feet. It is also the fallback when Aasgard or the trailhead is closed. From Lake Viviane, go up and right toward Temple Lake and then up climbers' paths through boulders to the base of the south face.
runs: up climbers paths through boulders to the base of

text: Follow the steep flake system on the left side of the big dihedral. It narrows to an airy spire right beside the corner; belay at or next to the spire. The flakes take good gear, but check them before loading.
runs: steep flake system on the left side of the

text: Starts just right of the outside corner on the left flank of the south face and climbs a right-leaning crack system to a stembox, a roof/hand-crack pitch, slabby/off-width terrain past a chimney (loose rock caution), and a final splitter corner crack, topping out on the West Ridge rather than the true summit.
runs: right of the outside corner on the left flank of the

text: A valid permit is required for both day and overnight use in the Enchantment Permit Area. Day permits are free and self-issued at the trailheads; overnight permits are issued by competitive lottery through Recreation.gov.
runs: self issued at the trailheads overnight permits are

text: Approach from Gnome Pond, hike the talus field to the base of the South Face, pass the Beckey-Davis route, and continue right.
runs: the talus field to the base of the south face pass the

text: There are two ways onto this peak and each has its own recognisable base. From the south, the base is the Ptarmigan-Dot saddle at about 7,800 ft, a genuine meadow holding a small tarn, unmistakable ground after miles of talus and the last water on the day. From that saddle the south slopes rise as open alpine tundra, scree and easy talus and there is nothing to find; you simply walk up. Getting to the saddle from the Shellrock Pass camp means gaining the crest north of camp and travelling over or around the shoulder of Mount Lago, with a short exposed step or two on the connecting ridge near the two rock points south of Dot. From the north and west the base is a saddle at about 7,250 ft overlooking Ptarmigan Lake, and the marker there is better still: a well-trodden boot path leaves the maintained trail at the Tatoosh Buttes junction around 6,950 ft and heads due south across the hillside and over a low rise on Tamarack Ridge, and following it to the saddle puts you at the foot of the north ridge, which is broad and easy. Whichever side you come from, the same rule identifies the route: the ground under you should stay rounded, open and tundra-covered. Ptarmigan's north face is sheer and seldom seen, so any point where the slope stops falling away gently and starts breaking off is the signal that you have wandered onto the wrong aspect and should move back south.
runs: heads due south across the hillside and over

text: The shortest line on the map, but it starts below 3,500 ft instead of high on the Slate Pass road. From the trailhead at the end of Eightmile Creek Road, cross Eightmile Pass and follow the trail past the Hidden Lakes to Ptarmigan Creek, northeast of the peak, then go a further two or three miles to the base. Expect a long day of trail before any climbing.
runs: to ptarmigan creek northeast of the peak then

text: From the saddle between Vesper and Wolf Peak, an obvious ledge system cuts across the north face at roughly 5,800 ft, starting at a small notch overlooking the Vesper Glacier. The climbing is sustained low-5th-class rock with the crux exposed traverse pitch reported on pitch 5 (some parties also flag a 5.7 slab on pitch 2); belays are a mix of fixed (bolted/pin) anchors and gear anchors atop pitches 1 and 3. No rappels are needed — parties walk off. Popular enough that other Vesper lines (e.g. True Grit) are sometimes used as a less-crowded backup.
runs: at a small notch overlooking the vesper glacier

text: Same trailhead and trail as True Grit: Sunrise Mine Trail #707 from the Sunrise Mine Trailhead on the Mountain Loop Highway, through second-growth forest and an early creek crossing of the South Fork Stillaguamish (log crossing, harder in high runoff), up through Wirtz Basin and out onto open, cairned talus, then through Headlee Pass (~4,720 ft, 2.7 mi, loose rock/rockfall exposure in the narrow couloir) and down to Vesper Creek and Vesper Lake (Lake Elan, ~5,000 ft, ~3.5 mi/~2,700 ft gain) — the last dependable water. From the lake the maintained trail fades; cross the outlet and follow an obvious talus ridgeline up to the saddle between Vesper and Wolf Peak, the small summit just northeast of Vesper. From there a slightly improbable but well-trodden heather ledge system (goat trail through it) cuts across the north face at roughly 5,800 ft to a small notch overlooking the remnant Vesper Glacier, where the route starts. This traverse crosses steep, exposed heather that's treacherous when wet and typically holds snow into mid-to-late summer, so an ice axe (and sometimes crampons) is worth carrying into early summer. Plan on 3+ hours from the trailhead to the base of the climb.
runs: and follow an obvious talus ridgeline up to

text: Climb a layback flake into a low-angle groove to 3rd-class slabs, gear belay below a faint white dyke splitting the slab above (Blue Line variation, better rock than the original start).
runs: a low angle groove to 3rd class slabs
gear belay below a faint white dyke splitting

text: Climb the dyke past three bolts to a thin ledge, then traverse right and up a short gully to the anchor.
runs: climb the dyke past three bolts to a thin ledge
traverse right and up a short gully to

text: Step right then traverse back left on positive edges toward the skyline; a single bolt and fixed pins protect a nice arête above.
runs: step right then traverse back left on positive edges

text: The crux pitch — step right and climb straight up in a very exposed position, taking gear well; at the second bolt, traverse right 50 ft to the anchor.
runs: at the second bolt traverse right 50 ft to

text: The "money pitch" — a long, easy romp up the exposed arête to the summit, capping the climb.
runs: the money pitch a long easy romp up the

text: From Marblemount, drive SR-20 east about 45 miles and turn right between mileposts 151 and 152 onto the short spur road signed for Easy Pass, which ends at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park, and camping on the national park side of the pass needs a backcountry permit.
runs: turn right between mileposts 151 and 152 onto

text: From the Easy Pass Trailhead on SR-20, hike the Easy Pass Trail about 3.5 miles and roughly 2,900 ft to Easy Pass, about 6,500 ft. Most parties then leave the trail and sidehill west along the south side of the ridge on grassy benches around 6,600-6,800 ft, crossing many small gullies and buttresses; a large gully with a waterfall just before the basin needs a short descent of steep scree. The usual high camp is in the basin just south of Mesahchie Peak at about 6,600-6,700 ft, roughly five hours from the car. The alternative is to follow the trail down the far side of the pass into the Fisher Creek basin near 5,100 ft and climb off-trail back up to the same camp. From camp, climb northwest to the Mesahchie-Katsuk saddle to start the traverse.
runs: in the basin just south of mesahchie peak

text:
This route is reached from high, not from low, and that single sentence separates it from the other line on this pinnacle.

There are two ways onto its ledge, described from opposite directions and they meet in the same place. Either cut right off the col trail before topping out, crossing a very loose slope to gain the left end of an obvious ledge system; or go all the way to the col and descend about three hundred feet along the pinnacle's flank to the same ledge. Both are quick.

Then walk the ledge rightward to its far end. This is the step people skip. The ledge is third class and it goes further than you expect; the route does not start where you step onto it. Keep going until the ledge runs out.

At the far right end of the ledge, a steep clean corner rises straight off it. That corner is the route. It is a big obvious corner system on the right side of the pinnacle's main face, and the climbing in it is continuous, clean and steep — the physical test is that the rock quality is conspicuously better than the loose slope you crossed to get there.

Confirm on the climb. Pitch one is moderate with a chimney-behind-a-block move. Pitch two is the standout: a steep continuous corner to a triangular roof, passed on finger locks. Pitch three is the hardest, off a detached flake into steep flaring finger and hand jams on the left wall. Pitch four is corner climbing into an offwidth section. A triangular roof on the second pitch and a detached flake on the third are the two features that settle it.

Negative marker: if you left the trail down at the bench around 6,600 ft, contoured right past a spring in a dry sandy gully, and found a chockstone at the toe of a ridge, you are at the other route on this pinnacle — several number grades easier and a different day. A chockstone at a ridge toe is not this climb; a corner at the far right end of a ledge is.

Second negative marker: the neighbouring spire's routes start from the col itself and are the usual link-up partner. Standing at the col with rock above you is not evidence you are here; you still have to lose height.

At the top, either scramble third-class ground north-east toward the neighbouring spire's north face to continue a link-up, downclimbing over precariously stacked blocks and flakes, or make two thirty-metre rappels down the gully back to the col.
runs: a very loose slope to gain the left end of an obvious ledge system
corner system on the right side of the

text: Rapple Grapple shares its first pitch with the Beckey Route, then traverses right along the 'Beckey ledge' past a few trees into an open-book corner system with 5.7 finger and hand cracks, rejoining the Beckey Route near the top of the buttress before the final scramble and 5.6 slab to the summit — a local guide favorite as a slightly harder alternative to the standard line.
runs: shares its first pitch with the beckey route

text: After the Beckey Route's first pitch, traverse right along the 'Beckey ledge' past a few trees and climb an open-book corner system to the top of the buttress, rejoining the Beckey Route. A direct start begins a few feet right of a red blocky overhang and trends left to rejoin the original line; another variation continues past the Beckey ledge to an overhanging leaning block with a tree belay before moving up and left to rejoin the route. Includes a 10-15 ft 5.8 crack with an old piton and finishes on a 10-ft 5.6 slab to the summit.
runs: the beckey ledge past a few trees and
an open book corner system to the top of the buttress rejoining the beckey route

text: From the Blue Lake Trailhead, hike the Blue Lake Trail ~1.5 miles to the meadow, then take the climbers' path left past the small stream up through slabs and talus toward the Liberty Bell-Concord gully. Rapple Grapple shares its first pitch with the Beckey Route, so follow the standard Beckey approach (stay right at the gully fork) to the same base.
runs: shares its first pitch with the beckey route

text: After finishing the route’s scramble and short 5.6 slab to the ridge, take the standard Liberty Bell descent, which lands close to the base of the route. From the summit, downclimb the upper pitch a short way and go left (east) to a tree hung with rappel slings. One single-rope rappel with a 60 m rope reaches a sandy ledge; work right and down to a bolted station, then make two single-rope rappels of about 25 m from bolted anchors into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft. Parties who downclimb the ridge and the 5.6 boulder problem to the first bolts instead of making the tree rappel do two rappels in all. From the notch, downclimb the loose gully back to the climbers’ path and the Blue Lake Trail.
runs: with rappel slings one single rope rappel with a
downclimb the ridge and the 5.6 boulder problem

text: Shares its first pitch with the Beckey Route: a low-fifth-class traverse and chimney past ledges and small trees to a belay at the base of a steeper chimney.
runs: shares its first pitch with the beckey route
chimney past ledges and small trees to a belay at the base of a steeper chimney

text:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead, hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to the meadow, then take the climbers' path left past the small stream up through slabs and talus toward the Liberty Bell-Concord gully.

Four pitches at 5.8. The route shares its first pitch with the Beckey Route, so the approach is the standard Beckey approach to the same base.
runs: shares its first pitch with the beckey route

text: From Twisp, drive WA-20 east a short distance to WA-153, then south on WA-153 to Libby Creek Road (County Road 1045), about 1.4 miles south of Carlton. Turn right and follow Libby Creek Road about 2.5 miles, turn left onto Forest Road 43 for about 5.1 miles, left onto Forest Road 4340 for about 1.2 miles, right onto Forest Road 4340-700 for about 1.5 miles, and left onto Forest Road 4340-750 for about 0.9 mile to the Libby Lake Trailhead (4,400–4,430 ft; roadside parking for roughly 10 vehicles, no toilet or potable water). From the trailhead, follow Libby Creek Trail #415 to Libby Lake, watching for trail damage (root holes) from the 2018 Crescent Mountain Fire between roughly miles 0.8 and 2.5. A dilapidated cabin sits beside the trail at about 7,170 ft, used by some parties as a base camp.
runs: 2.5 miles turn left onto forest road 43

text:
The gully above the lake is the route and it is the worst ground of the day - that is how you know you are on it. From the lake basin, the line ascends a very loose gully to gain the ridge crest. Parties routinely exit the gully about half-way up onto the rib that parallels it, because the rib holds more solid rock; the rib is an escape from the gully rather than an alternative to it, so if you cannot see the gully from the rib you have wandered.

If the ground you are climbing is pleasant, you are not in the right gully. Several chutes rise out of this basin; the one that is the route is the one that leads to the saddle on the crest.

The critical negative marker is on the ridge, not on the approach: a small peak stands just west of the saddle, and it is not the summit. Once on the crest the true high point is reached by an easy scramble eastward along the ridge. If you topped out of the gully and went left to a summit within a few minutes, you are on the lower point west of the saddle.

The positive test at the top is the walk. The true summit is a ridge scramble away over talus and large boulders, with intervening bumps, rather than an immediate high point above the gully. Ground you can traverse in minutes is the wrong answer here.

Also note the name trap in the roads and lakes on this side of the range: the drainage this variant uses and the one the south-east ridge uses have similarly named creeks and lakes on the same forest road system, so navigate by the road numbers and the trailhead you actually parked at rather than by the name of a lake.
runs: ascends a very loose gully to gain the ridge

text: At about 8,200 ft climb out of the gully to the left onto the rib, where the rock is appreciably more solid, and follow it to the ridge crest at roughly 8,473 ft. Staying in the gully to its top is the common mistake; the rib is both safer and faster. Grade is easy scrambling, class 2+ at most.
runs: climb out of the gully to the left

text: From the summit, downclimb the upper ridge scrambling to the first gendarme, rappel its west side, continue down the ridge to the second gendarme, rappel it, then scramble down and around the west slope on boulders and scree, bypassing the North Summit, back to the high camp at ~7,500 ft; from there retrace the bushwhack to Remmel Lake.
runs: scramble down and around the west slope on

text: Follow the ridge top as much as possible to the first of the two main gendarmes, and climb it in a couple of short pitches rated 5.1 to 5.2 on mostly stable rock. Harder variations exist. Protection is a small rack of nuts and long slings. On the way down, this gendarme needs a rappel.
runs: follow the ridge top as much as possible

text: From Twisp, drive west up the Twisp River Road (FR 44) for 18.3 miles and bear left onto FR 4435. Cross the Twisp River in 0.3 mile, turn right after the bridge to stay on FR 4435, drive 1.1 miles upriver and turn left onto Spur 4435-015, reaching the trailhead in another 0.3 mile at about 3,100 ft. A free self-issued Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness permit is filled out at the kiosk.
runs: 4435 drive 1.1 miles upriver and turn left

text: Once you have reached the summit of East Fury, you may continue to West Fury via this traverse. The traverse is a series of gendarmes and towers with a combination of scrambling and low 5th class rock. The descent off East Fury to the low saddle is on very loose Class 2-3 boulders. There are three towers you must climb up and over before making the final ascent to the summit of West Fury. A 50-60 meter rope is recommended at the very least for rappelling the 4th and low 5th class areas you have climbed.

text: From the Big Beaver landing, follow the nearly flat Big Beaver Trail about 9.4 miles up the valley to Luna Camp. About a mile and a half beyond camp, leave the trail on a small boot path and cross Big Beaver Creek just north of the Access Creek confluence, around 2,460 ft. Depending on the year this is a log or a wade.
runs: and cross big beaver creek just north of

text: Drive SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) to the Ross Dam Trailhead and walk down to Ross Lake, where most parties take the paid water taxi from Ross Lake Resort to the Big Beaver landing rather than walking the lakeshore trail. From the landing it is about 9.4 miles of nearly flat old-growth trail up the Big Beaver valley to Luna Camp, the usual first night. About a mile and a half beyond camp, leave the trail on a small boot path and cross Big Beaver Creek just north of where Access Creek comes in, around 2,460 ft. Depending on the year this is a log or a wade. Then climb the north side of Access Creek on a faint, brushy climbers' path through Access Creek basin, up the south gully and around the south side of Luna Peak to Luna Col, the usual high camp. From Luna Col, follow the ridge toward Fury over class 3 ground with many short ups and downs. Drop to traverse heather slopes on its south side to the Southeast Glacier near 6,700 ft, then climb the right side of the glacier to steeper snow and a possible bergschrund below East Fury's summit, where the traverse to the West Peak begins. Allow three to five days for the round trip. The Luna Fire closure has shut the Big Beaver Trail from Big Beaver Stock Camp to Stillwell Camp, including Luna Camp, and bars cross-country travel from the closed trail; check the park's current fire closures before planning.
runs: and cross big beaver creek just north of where access creek

text: A 50-60 m rope at minimum, for rappelling the 4th- and low-5th-class sections between the three towers. Plan on building and leaving anchors: the rock is chossy, solid placements are scarce, and the rappels on this traverse go off poor-quality anchors - so carry slings and rings to back them up. Each rappel you make on the way across makes retreat progressively harder.
runs: for rappelling the 4th and low 5th class

text: Two approach pitches (bolted 5.8 slab, then low-5th groove) lead to the base of the actual Roan Wall from this point.
runs: to the base of the actual roan wall

text: About 14 quickdraws plus a single set of nuts and cams to 2 inches; all belays have new double-ring stainless steel bolted anchors.
runs: a single set of nuts and cams to 2

text: Scramble a short way up the gully above the slab, then climb a low-fifth-class groove on the right side of a brushy wall to reach the foot of the orange-and-grey main face. The ground is dirty and vegetated and is the one pitch low on the route without bolts; it is slick when wet.
runs: groove on the right side of a brushy wall

text: Edges, mantles and cracks straight up to the top of the wall. From the top, the descent is by rappel down the route on the bolted double-ring anchors; the face below is clean and open, and two ropes are the recommended setup.
runs: edges mantles and cracks straight up to the top

text: Up a bit, then right on the obvious ledge to belay at the base of the main slab.
runs: on the obvious ledge to belay at the base of the main slab

text: Nice face pitch right and up past a 10a friction crux; 9 bolts.
runs: nice face pitch right and up past a 10a friction crux 9 bolts

text: Sustained face pitch stepping right then up, weaving around small corners and features; 8 bolts.
runs: right then up weaving around small corners and features 8 bolts

text: Angle left for three bolts then step right across a shallow corner to a knobby section; 9 bolts.
runs: angle left for three bolts then step right across a shallow corner

text: Another full pitch of classic slabbing with crimpy holds; 8 bolts.
runs: another full pitch of classic slabbing with crimpy holds 8 bolts

text: Angle backs off for a unique final pitch: an overlap with a 4-inch crack (bolt above), step left past a small tree to an awkward 5.8 ramp/crack, low-angle face, then an easy off-width to the belay.
runs: low angle face then an easy off width to the belay

text: From the Robinson Creek Trailhead, follow the maintained Robinson Creek Trail north, cross Beauty Creek, and turn uphill onto the unmarked, unmaintained Beauty Creek Trail. Climb the brushy, steep Beauty Creek valley, cross a tributary around 5,200-5,260 ft, then ascend open meadow/scree to a small tarn at roughly 6,750-6,800 ft in a rocky basin. From the tarn, climb the loose scree slope (snow-covered in early season) north of the tarn to a gap in the southeast ridge, then turn left (north-west) and follow the ridge about a mile over several false summits — mostly class 2 walking with a few class 3 sections and a narrow, exposed crux just below the true summit.
runs: the loose scree slope snow covered in early season north of the tarn to a gap in the southeast ridge

text: From Winthrop, drive Highway 20 west about 15 miles and turn right onto Lost River Road (County Road 9140). After half a mile turn left to stay on Lost River Road, drive 7.5 paved miles, then continue about 1.25 miles on gravel Forest Road 5400 to the Robinson Creek Trailhead on the right, at about 2,500 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed to park.
runs: turn left to stay on lost river road

text: From Winthrop, drive Highway 20 west about 14-15 miles to the Mazama junction, then turn onto Lost River Road (County Road 9140) and drive about 7.5 paved miles and another 1.5 miles on gravel Forest Road 5400 to Robinson Creek Trailhead (elev. ~2,500-2,560 ft, with an information sign, picnic table, and vault toilet). From the trailhead, hike the Robinson Creek - Middle Fork Trail (#478) north for about 2.8 miles to the signed/bridged Beauty Creek junction (elev. ~3,560 ft) just past a bridge over Beauty Creek. Turn right (northeast/uphill) onto the unmarked, overgrown Beauty Creek Trail and follow it about 1.5 miles up the valley, staying northwest of the creek, to a tributary crossing around 5,200-5,260 ft, then continue up open slopes to the tarn basin at about 6,750-6,800 ft.
runs: another 1.5 miles on gravel forest road 5400 to

text: Ascend the loose scree slope north of the tarn to a gap in the southeast ridge.
runs: north of the tarn to a gap in the southeast ridge

text:
Drive Highway 20 west from Winthrop about fifteen miles, right onto Lost River Road, a half mile then left to stay on it, seven and a half paved miles and another mile and a quarter of gravel FR 5400 to the Robinson Creek trailhead on the right. The trailhead sits at 2,500 to 2,600 ft. Ballard Campground is a minute or two away and is the standard car-camp.

Walk the Robinson Creek trail #478 — an easy valley walk through big timber — about two and eight tenths miles to the Beauty Creek junction near 3,560 to 3,600 ft. Mileages for it range from two to two and eight tenths, so use the elevation and the landmark rather than a mile count.

The landmark is the second bridge, the one over Beauty Creek, with Beauty Creek Falls cascading beside it. The junction is thirty to a hundred feet past that bridge, on the uphill side, and it is unmarked. Two parties independently warn that it is far less obvious than you would expect, one describing it as covered in bushes and nearly walked past. If you get thirty feet beyond the bridge and have not seen it, stop, go back, and look up on climber's right.

Beauty Creek #579 — not #479, which is a different trail entirely — is unmaintained and does not appear on maps. It stays on the west and north-west side of the creek the whole way. One party notes their topo showed it on the east side and the topo was wrong; that is a usable check. Blowdown is the recurring nuisance, typically five to nine logs.

Total for the peak is fourteen to fifteen miles with somewhere between 6,200 and 6,900 ft of gain, and four separate parties report ten to fourteen hours car to car as a single day.
runs: gravel fr 5400 to the robinson creek trailhead on the right

text: Park at a turnout across from a large boulder field on the northwest side of the mountain. Climb steeply up the hillside left (east) of the boulder field to gain the northwest ridge, follow it over Point 6315', transition onto the west ridge around 5,400 ft, and finish with a scramble up the summit ridge. In snow season, cliff bands along the ridge are typically turned via snow ramps.
runs: from a large boulder field on the northwest side of

text: Head southeast up the open ridge over Point 6315'. The last several hundred feet to the summit ridge are steep, with cornices along the crest overhanging the north face - stay well back from the edge, keeping to the trees while they last. A breakable wind crust over powder can make this slow going. Small glaciers lie on the north side of the summit ridge.
runs: on the north side of the summit ridge

text: From Colonial Creek Campground, follow the popular Thunder Creek Trail and then Fourth of July Pass Trail to the broad, forested pass at ~3,600 ft. At the pass, an unsigned, unmaintained path (the old 'Ruby Mountain Way Trail') marked by a jagged 8-ft stump and orange flagging on the north side of the main trail climbs through deadfall and heather benches onto the open south ridge, finishing on wide-open scree and talus to the summit. Non-technical but long, with real route-finding difficulty in the mid-mountain deadfall zone.
runs: on the north side of the main trail

text: At Fourth of July Pass, look for a jagged 8-ft stump with orange flagging on the north side of the main trail — it marks the start of the old Ruby Mountain Way Trail.
runs: on the north side of the main trail

text: From Marblemount, drive SR 20 east about 24 miles; just past milepost 130, before crossing the Thunder Arm of Diablo Lake, turn into the south side of Colonial Creek Campground and park in the large lot above the boat ramp. Walk the length of the campground, following signs to the amphitheater, where the Thunder Creek Trail begins. Hike the Thunder Creek Trail roughly 1.7-2.1 miles to the Fourth of July Pass Trail junction, then continue steeply up the west slopes about 5.2 miles total (2,629 ft gain) to Fourth of July Pass.
runs: before crossing the thunder arm of diablo lake turn

text: Old trail switchbacks up the south ridge through sparse forest, then a long leftward traverse across grassy benches and heather slopes with tight switchbacks.
runs: a long leftward traverse across grassy benches and

text: Above 4,950 ft the path switchbacks north through sparse forest on the south ridge, then makes a long leftward traverse across grassy benches and moderate heather, then up a steep southwest-facing heather slope on tight switchbacks. Above about 6,600 ft it becomes scree and talus and the ridge opens out — wide enough that it can be walked without a trail to the gentle summit ridge near 7,400 ft. Steep heather is slick when wet or frosted and holds snow late; snow on these slopes turns a walk-up into a self-arrest problem, so carry an axe outside of high summer.
runs: a long leftward traverse across grassy benches and moderate heather

text: Approach via the maintained Hannegan Pass Trail to Hannegan Pass, then follow an unmaintained climbers' trail south onto the Ruth Glacier and up easy snow to Ruth Mountain's summit. From Ruth, descend about 1,600 ft in two roughly 800-ft steps to the low saddle between Ruth and Icy, cross talus and glacier to a notch west of Icy's Northwest Spire near 6,500 ft, then climb roughly 500 ft of 2nd-3rd class terrain and a short 4th class summit gully to Icy Peak. The whole traverse is reversed to descend.
runs: to the low saddle between ruth and icy

text: Shares its trailhead and lower approach with the South Slopes/Ruth Glacier route: Hannegan Pass Trail #674 from the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (end of FR-32) up the Ruth Creek valley to Hannegan Pass (5,066 ft, ~4 miles, ~2,000 ft gain), then the climbers' path east and south past the pond below the pass (faint, easy to lose), around a cliff-band shoulder, and onto the Ruth Glacier's north slope to a camp near the notch northwest of Ruth's summit (~6,600 ft) — see the South Slopes route for full trailhead-to-glacier detail, including the documented crevasse-fall hazard on the lower glacier despite its mellow appearance. From camp, the traverse is conventionally done Ruth-to-Icy: tag Ruth's summit first, then descend roughly 800 ft south and west toward a gully on the peak's west side, pick up a faint boot path, and continue down another ~800 ft (about 1,600 ft total off Ruth's summit) to the low saddle/col between Ruth and Icy at roughly 5,700-5,800 ft. Parties choose between a steeper, more direct 'death gully' line or supposedly-cairned heather slopes and game trails to climber's left holding 2nd-3rd class ground — the heather-slope option is the safer, recommended line. From the saddle, cross a patch of trees and talus/boot-path along the connecting ridge to the Icy Glacier, then ascend talus and slabs below a rock ridge to gain the glacier proper, aiming for a notch/saddle just west of Icy's Northwest Spire (~6,500 ft). From that notch it's another ~500 ft of 2nd-3rd class scrambling up an obvious left-hand, light-colored gully system to the base of Icy's summit block, where a 100-ft, 4th-class gully (solid jugs and ledges but real exposure) leads to the top. Helmets are standard here given loose rock and traffic funneled through a single gully. Note the true (highest) summit is the SE point, about 11 ft higher than the peak most maps label as the top.
runs: ascend talus and slabs below a rock ridge

text:
Shares its trailhead and lower approach with the Ruth Glacier route: Trail #674 from the Hannegan Pass Trailhead up Ruth Creek to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft, then the faint climbers' path east and south past the pond, around the cliff-band shoulder, and onto the Ruth Glacier's north slope to a camp near the notch northwest of Ruth's summit around 6,600 ft.

The traverse is conventionally done Ruth-to-Icy: tag Ruth's summit first, then descend roughly 800 ft south and west toward a gully on the peak's west side, pick up a faint boot path, and continue down another 800 ft or so — about 1,600 ft in total off Ruth's summit — to the low saddle between Ruth and Icy at roughly 5,700-5,800 ft.

From the saddle, cross a patch of trees and follow talus and boot path along the connecting ridge to the Icy Glacier, then talus and slabs below a rock ridge to gain the glacier proper.

The re-ascent of Ruth on the way home is the sting in the tail and cannot be avoided on the standard car-to-car version.
runs: to the low saddle between ruth and icy

text: From the saddle, cross a patch of trees and talus/boot-path along the connecting ridge to the Icy Glacier, then ascend talus and slabs below a rock ridge to gain the glacier proper, aiming for a notch/saddle just west of Icy's Northwest Spire (~6,500 ft).

text: This is the important one. Everything from Hannegan Pass south along the ridge to the base of the Ruth Glacier is Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, so no national park backcountry permit is required here — only the parking pass at the trailhead. The park boundary lies above and beyond, so a party that camps on this ridge and climbs Ruth as a day trip avoids the park permit system entirely. Standard wilderness rules apply: small groups, no fires at this elevation in practice, pack out everything.
runs: ridge to the base of the ruth glacier

text: The Boston Basin approach starts at an unmarked climbers' pullout on Cascade River Road roughly 21.5-23 miles from Marblemount (about 3,200-3,300 ft) - there's no formal trailhead sign, so watch your odometer. From the pullout, follow an old mining road/track for about a mile with minimal elevation gain, crossing Boston Creek. Watch closely for the unmaintained climbers' trail breaking off sharply to the right (cairns/flagging mark it, but it's easy to walk past); it climbs steeply through forest and a brushy old avalanche-slide path with sections of deadfall and loose footing. The path gains roughly 2,500 ft over about 2.5-3 miles to reach treeline and the lower Boston Basin camp (~5,300-5,400 ft), continuing to established upper camps around 6,200 ft. Plan on 3-4 hours trailhead to camp. Because this is a genuine climbers' path rather than a maintained trail, route-finding through the lower forest and slide-alder sections is the main approach hazard, and it can be greasy and slick when wet. Water is available from Boston Creek and seasonal snowmelt through mid-summer near camp. From high camp, rope up around 6,700 ft and make a rising traverse near the cliffs below Sharkfin Tower, picking a line up the Quien Sabe Glacier while avoiding crevasses - two common ascent lines (a left-side line and a more direct one) merge partway up. Expect to navigate a bergschrund via snow bridges around 7,600 ft and again near 8,100 ft, where large open crevasses flank the route on both sides in late season, before climbing to the Boston-Sahale col. From the col, a short but exposed snow traverse (crampons and axe recommended even late season) leads to the base of the summit block, finished with class 3-4 scrambling to the true summit.
runs: make a rising traverse near the cliffs below sharkfin

text: Make a rising traverse near the cliffs below Sharkfin Tower. The left (north) side is broken but moderate; a more direct line to the right is steeper and more crevassed. The two lines merge about halfway up, where a line must be picked between crevasses on the steeper upper glacier. Pickets are useful on the steeper snow.
runs: make a rising traverse near the cliffs below sharkfin

text: From the col, traverse right (south) across a short but exposed snow slope to the base of the summit block, with a short rocky step between snow sections. Keep crampons and axe for it even late in the season. A large cornice persists on the ridge into early summer, so stay well off its edge.
runs: slope to the base of the summit block

text: Early-mid September is reportedly completely dry aside from the glacier, but the bergschrund and crevasses open up more, requiring route-finding to climber's right to end-run the bergschrund
runs: to climber's right to end run the bergschrund

text:
Drive Cascade River Road about 21.7 miles from Marblemount to the Boston Basin fork at roughly 3,200-3,300 ft. There is no trailhead sign — it is an unmarked pullout, so watch the odometer rather than looking for signage.

Walk the old Diamond Mine roadbed for about three quarters of a mile to a mile, past the derelict mine site, with almost no elevation gain. The point people miss is where the climbers' trail leaves the roadbed sharply to the right and goes straight up; it is cairned and flagged but easy to walk past.

Above that the path is steep and unmaintained, switchbacking through forest and a brushy old slide path with deadfall, and crossing four small streams over roughly the next half mile — that is the last reliable water before camp, so fill there. Treeline comes at about 5,300 ft. Low camp sits on heather benches around 5,300-5,700 ft; the higher camp on a meadow knoll at about 6,200-6,400 ft cuts real time off summit day.

From camp, stay on climber's left toward the left side of Sharkfin Tower, rope up around 6,700 ft, and make a rising traverse under the cliffs below Sharkfin onto a flatter part of the Quien Sabe, then pick a line up the steeper section. Two common lines (one further left, one more direct) merge partway up.

Boston Basin is a cross-country zone; overnight permits are picked up in person at Marblemount. Biting flies are notorious here in midsummer.
runs: the left side of sharkfin tower rope up

text: Saska Peak is the third-highest peak in the Chelan Mountains and rises just northwest of its taller neighbor Emerald Peak (8,422 ft), 0.66 mi away across a connecting col. It's almost always climbed in combination with Emerald via that col, and strong parties often add Cardinal Peak (1.5 mi southeast) for a three-summit outing sometimes called the Entiat Bulgers. The peak sits deep in the North Fork Entiat River drainage inside Glacier Peak Wilderness — a long, quiet approach through fire-damaged forest rewards climbers with a genuinely remote basin and, in October, larch color on the descent.

text: P1-2: relatively clean, though loose/breaking rock is still possible. P2 has a sustained steep hand crack with awesome exposure. P3: a tempting finger crack directly above the belay has two large sharp flakes to its left that could cut the rope or fall on the belayer; the leftward traverse above is simple but must be done delicately due to numerous loose blocks (fist to cooler size). P4: several large loose blocks between the fixed piton at the start and the left edge of a large roof, including one thigh-sized block next to the hand crack above the slab; cleaner above and around the roof. P5+: finishing pitches are blocky and less loose.
